scalars-vectors-s1.title: A walk along a hallway
scalars-vectors-s1.text: Tape marks every meter along a straight hallway, with positive to the right. Mia starts at x = +2 m, walks to the 7 m mark (leg 1), turns around and walks to the 0 m mark (leg 2). The walk takes 20 s in all.
scalars-vectors-s1.html: Key: dashed arrows show the path of each leg; the faded figure marks the start.

scalars-vectors-s2.title: A delivery robot in a corridor
scalars-vectors-s2.text: A delivery robot moves along a straight corridor. East is positive. In each leg it moves at a steady speed; between legs it turns around or keeps going. The table lists each leg's displacement and how long it took.

items.q: What total distance does Mia walk?

mistakes.why: Value: 2 m is the size of her displacement (start to end). Distance counts every meter walked: 5 m out and 7 m back.
Value: 5 m is leg 1 alone. Distance adds every leg: 5 m out plus 7 m back.

why.correct: Distance adds the length of every leg, with no signs: 5.0 m (from 2 m to 7 m) + 7.0 m (from 7 m to 0 m) = 12 m.

items.q: What is Mia's displacement for the whole walk? Use a negative number for a displacement to the left.

mistakes.why: Value: 12 m is the distance, the length of her path. Displacement only compares where she ended (0 m) with where she started (+2 m).
Value: −7 m is only leg 2. Displacement for the whole walk compares the final position with the very first one.

why.correct: Displacement is the final position minus the starting position: 0 m − (+2 m) = −2.0 m. The minus sign says it points left.

items.q: How does the size of Mia's displacement compare with the distance she walks?
options: It is equal, because both describe the same walk
It is larger, because displacement includes a direction
It is smaller, because displacement is measured in a different unit
It is smaller, because she reversed direction partway

why.correct: Distance is 12 m; the displacement is −2.0 m, size 2.0 m. Turning around makes the displacement smaller than the distance.
options: They match only for a trip in one direction. Mia turned around, so the two differ.
A direction does not add size. The size of a displacement can never be more than the path length.
Both are measured in meters; the difference comes from turning around, not from units.
Right: the 5 m out and most of the way back cancel in the displacement, but every meter counts toward distance.

items.q: During leg 2, what is the sign of Mia's velocity?
options: Positive, because she is still at positive positions
Positive, because speed is a positive number
Negative, because she moves toward smaller x
Zero, because she ends up back near the start

why.correct: With right as positive, moving left means the velocity is negative, even while her position is still a positive number.
options: The sign of the velocity depends on the direction of motion, not on whether the position is positive.
Speed is the size of the velocity and has no sign; the velocity has the sign of the direction.
Right: her position decreases during leg 2, so her velocity points in the negative direction.
She is moving the whole time during leg 2; a zero velocity would mean she stands still.

items.q: After leg 2, Mia walks a third leg so that her displacement for the entire walk becomes zero. Where does she finish?
options: At the 0 m mark
At the +2 m mark
At the +7 m mark
At the −2 m mark

why.correct: Zero displacement for the whole walk means she ends where she began, at +2 m (a third leg of +2.0 m).
options: That is where leg 2 ended; staying there leaves a displacement of −2.0 m.
Right: zero displacement means the final position equals the starting position, +2 m.
That is where she turned around; it gives a displacement of +5.0 m from the start.
This walks another 2 m left, doubling the displacement to −4.0 m instead of cancelling it.

items.q: What total distance does the robot travel in the four legs?

mistakes.why: Value: 1.5 m is the displacement, where the signs cancel. Distance adds every leg as a positive length.

why.correct: Distance adds the sizes of all four legs: 12.0 + 5.5 + 9.0 + 14.0 = 40.5 m.

items.q: What is the robot's total displacement? Give a signed value (east is positive).

mistakes.why: Value: 40.5 m is the distance. A displacement adds the legs as vectors, so the westward legs are negative.
Value: 21 m adds only the eastward legs. The westward legs are negative and must be added too.

why.correct: Add the displacements with their signs: +12.0 − 5.5 + 9.0 − 14.0 = +1.5 m, so the robot ends 1.5 m east of where it started.

items.q: In which leg does the robot have the greatest speed?
options: Leg 1
Leg 2
Leg 4
Leg 3

why.correct: Speed is the size of the velocity. Leg speeds: 1.5, 1.1, 1.5 and 2.0 m/s. The negative sign of leg 4 shows direction, not slowness.
options: Leg 1 has the largest displacement east among the first three legs, but 12.0 m in 8.0 s is only 1.5 m/s.
Leg 2 covers 5.5 m in 5.0 s, 1.1 m/s, the slowest leg.
Right: 14.0 m in 7.0 s is 2.0 m/s, faster than any other leg; its velocity is −2.0 m/s because it moves west.
Leg 3 covers 9.0 m in 6.0 s, 1.5 m/s. A large positive value is not the same as the greatest speed.

items.q: What is the robot's velocity during leg 2? Give a signed value in m/s (east is positive).

mistakes.why: Value: you divided the time by the displacement. Velocity is displacement divided by time.

why.correct: Velocity = displacement ÷ time = (−5.5 m) ÷ (5.0 s) = −1.1 m/s: 1.1 m/s toward the west.

items.q: The robot makes a fifth leg that takes it back to exactly where it started. What is the displacement of that leg?
options: 0 m

why.correct: Returning to the start makes the total displacement zero: +1.5 m + (−1.5 m) = 0.
options: Right: the first four legs add to +1.5 m, so a fifth leg of −1.5 m brings the total to zero.
This doubles the displacement to +3.0 m instead of cancelling it; the return leg points the other way.
This undoes the distance, not the displacement; the robot is only 1.5 m from its start.
A leg with zero displacement leaves the robot 1.5 m east of its start.

items.q: Which of these quantities is a scalar?
options: The displacement of a runner
The velocity of a runner
The position of a runner on a track
The distance a runner covers

why.correct: A scalar has a size only. Distance and speed are scalars; position, displacement and velocity are vectors.
options: Displacement has a direction: it points from the start to the end.
Velocity is speed with a direction, so it is a vector.
Position is measured from an origin in a chosen direction, so it carries a sign: a vector.
Right: distance is a size only, with no direction.

items.q: A bus drives 235 m north along a straight street, then 410 m south. Taking north as positive, what is its total displacement?

mistakes.why: Value: 645 m is the distance driven. For displacement, the southward leg is negative.
Value: the size is right, but the bus ends south of its start, so with north positive the displacement is −175 m.

why.correct: Add the displacements with signs: +235 m + (−410 m) = −175 m, that is, 175 m south of the start.

items.q: Two cyclists ride along the same straight road at 6.0 m/s, one heading east and one heading west. Which statement is correct?
options: They have equal speeds and equal velocities
They have equal speeds but different velocities
They have different speeds but equal velocities
They have different speeds and different velocities

why.correct: Velocity is a vector: +6.0 m/s and −6.0 m/s (east positive) are different velocities with the same speed, 6.0 m/s.
options: Velocity includes direction; opposite directions mean different velocities.
Right: speed has no direction, so it matches; velocity includes direction, so it differs.
Both cover 6.0 m each second, so their speeds are equal, and their velocities point opposite ways.
Their speeds match: both are 6.0 m/s. Only the directions differ.

items.q: Which statement about a trip along a straight road is correct?
options: The size of the displacement is at most equal to the distance
The distance is at most equal to the size of the displacement
The distance and the size of the displacement are equal for a trip that ends where it started
The size of the displacement grows each time the traveler turns around

why.correct: Distance counts every meter of the path; displacement compares the ends. They are equal only for a trip in one direction.
options: Right: the straight-line change in position is the shortest way between the ends, so it cannot exceed the path length.
This reverses the rule; turning around adds distance without adding displacement.
A round trip has zero displacement but a nonzero distance.
Turning around brings the traveler back toward the start, which can shrink the displacement.

items.q: A ball sits at x = −3.0 m on a number line where east is positive. A student redraws the axis with the same origin but west as positive. What is the ball's position now?
options: 0 m

why.correct: The ball is 3.0 m west of the origin either way. With west positive, that is written +3.0 m. Positions depend on the coordinate system you choose.
options: The sign of a position depends on which direction is chosen as positive; flipping the axis flips the sign.
Only the direction was changed, not the origin, so the ball is still 3.0 m from it.
Changing the positive direction flips the sign; it does not move the ball 3.0 m farther away.
Right: the ball has not moved, but with west positive its location 3.0 m west of the origin is written +3.0 m.

items.q: A runner's velocity is −4.2 m/s, with east positive. What is the runner's speed?

mistakes.why: Value: speed is the size of the velocity and is never negative. Drop the sign: 4.2 m/s.

why.correct: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity, the size without the sign: 4.2 m/s. The minus sign only tells you the runner is heading west.
